summary:
Gombe State criminalises same-sex conduct under its own Shari'a Penal Code Law 2001, signed into law on 23 November 2001. The enacted statutory text covers conduct by men and women and reaches beyond Nigeria's federal criminal code. Human Rights Watch's 2004 report on Shari'a implementation lists Gombe among the twelve northern states that had adopted Shari'a into criminal legislation by 2002, with Shari'a courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond the federal code.

The penalties set by the state statute are severe and gendered. Unmarried men convicted of sodomy face caning of 100 lashes plus one year's imprisonment, and married men face stoning to death (rajm). The lesbianism offence carries up to 50 lashes plus imprisonment of up to six months. Gombe's own formulation defines gross indecency as any sexual offence against the normal or usual standards of behaviour.

The UK Home Office country-of-origin information note of June 2025 states that Islamic law applies to Muslims in the twelve northern states, which include Gombe, and criminalises same-sex sexual acts both between men and between women. It records the maximum penalty for 'sodomy' between men as death in all twelve states, with penalties for 'lesbianism' ranging from death to flogging and imprisonment. The note carries a dedicated section on enforcement of Shari'a provisions and on the attitude of the hisbah, the morality police.

Enforcement in Gombe is documented through a single mass operation. In October 2023 the Gombe State Command of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps raided a gathering at Duwa Plaza along the Bauchi-Gombe Expressway that was preparing a same-sex wedding, arresting 76 people. State spokesperson Buhari Sa'ad told reporters that 59 males were detained, 21 of whom wilfully confessed to being homosexuals, and that 17 females were present at the scene; the command stated that the detainees would be charged in court for a crime of social vice in Gombe State.

The Guardian of 23 October 2023, byline James Agberebi, independently confirmed the operation from Lagos press, reporting that the arrests followed a tip-off about a same-sex birthday party and planned marriage. Gombe NSCDC Commandant Mohammed Muazu confirmed the arrests; the spokesperson said the remaining males and the 17 females were invited guests and onlookers, and officers voiced concern over the participants' ages. Detention therefore reached people present at a gathering rather than only those alleged to have engaged in conduct. The most recent documented enforcement action in this record is this October 2023 raid; no later instance is documented.
tangentialFactors:
Gombe's sodomy offence is not a local drafting accident. The identical provision, 100 lashes plus one year for unmarried men and stoning for married men, appears in Jigawa, Kano and Zamfara, which points to a shared statutory template across four northern states rather than an isolated Gombe measure.

The October 2023 raid was carried out by a state command of a national security and civil-defence corps, not by a Shari'a court, and the charge announced was framed as social vice. Moral-crimes enforcement in Gombe thus runs through ordinary criminal procedure as well as through the Shari'a courts, which widens the range of agencies a visitor can be processed by.

Women were drawn into the same operation: 17 females were detained at the scene and were characterised by the command as invited guests and onlookers. The gendered reach of the statute's lesbianism offence is matched in practice by the detention of women who were not alleged to have committed anything.

The inventory contains no trans-specific violence figure for Gombe State, and no per-capita or population denominator for the state's enforcement actions, so the October 2023 arrest count cannot be ranked against other jurisdictions.
localsOnly:
Shari'a courts in Gombe hold criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond the federal code, a position recorded by Human Rights Watch in 2004 for the twelve northern states that had adopted Shari'a into criminal legislation by 2002. Muslim residents are therefore answerable to a second criminal layer that does not apply to non-Muslims.

The hisbah, the morality police, operates within the enforcement environment described for the twelve northern states, and the June 2025 UK Home Office note devotes a section to the attitude of the hisbah towards Shari'a provisions. Residents live under that standing presence in a way that short-term visitors do not.

Public identification by authorities is documented. In October 2023 the state command's spokesperson told reporters that 21 of the 59 detained males wilfully confessed to being homosexuals, placing those individuals' status on the record through an official briefing.

The statute's gross indecency clause, defined as any sexual offence against the normal or usual standards of behaviour, is written in Gombe's own formulation and supplies a broad local moral-crimes charge alongside the specific sodomy and lesbianism offences.
